segments.caption: In many shops, a small group of customers brings in most of the money.
Often, just 20% of the customers bring in 80% of the sales.
That's the Pareto distribution.
Here's the definition, in simple words.
In a Pareto distribution, most values are small.
But a few values are huge.
So the shape starts high, and stretches into a long tail on the right.
It's the idea behind the famous 80/20 rule.
Take a shop's customers, and line them up from the biggest spender to the smallest.
Now split them into 10 equal groups. Each group is 10% of the customers.
The top group alone brings in 73% of all the sales.
Add the second group, and the top 20% bring in 80%.
And the whole bottom half? Only about 9%.
Compare that with height.
Heights cluster around an average. Nobody is ten times taller than you.
But one customer can spend a hundred times more than another.
That's the long tail: rare, but enormous values.
This makes the average misleading.
The average customer spends about 1,400 rupees.
But the typical customer, the one in the middle, spends only about 360.
In fact, 9 out of 10 customers spend less than the average.
So for long-tailed data, the median tells you more.
A few people hold most of the wealth. A few cities are giant. A few videos get most of the views. And a few bugs cause most of the crashes.
So remember: most values are small, a few are huge, and the tail is long.
The top 20% often hold about 80%. But that's a rule of thumb, not a law.
Quick quiz!
An app's crashes come from many bugs, and they follow the 80/20 rule.
If the team fixes the top 20% of bugs, about how many crashes disappear?
About 80%!
The top 20% of causes bring about 80% of the effect. So fix the big ones first.
